claims.text: Write-Ahead Logging does not enable concurrent writes—only one writer transaction can hold the write lock at any moment. While WAL allows readers to operate simultaneously with a writer (reducing reader-writer conflicts), multiple writers must still serialize completely. This means high-write-throughput systems cannot achieve higher absolute write rates by switching to WAL.

claims.text: Checkpoint frequency creates a direct tradeoff: more frequent checkpoints keep the WAL file smaller (improving read performance since readers must check fewer pages) but increase checkpoint overhead; less frequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost over more writes (improving write performance) but slow reads. The default strategy runs automatic checkpoints at approximately 1000 pages (~4 MB), and this threshold is tunable based on application priorities.

claims.text: In rollback journal mode, a write transaction acquires an exclusive lock on the database file, preventing all readers from starting new transactions; readers conversely acquire a shared lock that blocks any new writers. This mutual exclusion means only one type of operation can proceed at any moment. WAL inverts this by having writers append to a separate file while readers continue accessing the unchanged main database. Each reader captures the highest WAL frame present when its transaction begins, and sees a consistent snapshot from that point forward, even as subsequent writes append new frames beyond that snapshot. The result: unlimited concurrent readers plus a single writer can all operate simultaneously without blocking each other.

claims.text: Under rollback journal, an active reader holding a shared lock blocks any writer from starting a new transaction, and any active writer blocks all new readers from connecting. WAL allows each transaction to capture an independent snapshot boundary at its start moment. When an analytics query begins, it records the current highest WAL frame number; that reader then only sees pages committed up to that frame, even as subsequent writes add new frames to the WAL after the query started. Long-running analytics can now continue uninterrupted while operational writes proceed independently, enabling production systems to run heavy analytics without degrading transaction latency.

claims.text: WAL introduces checkpoint starvation, a failure mode absent from rollback journals. Checkpoints move committed frames from the WAL back to the main database but cannot overwrite frames that older still-active readers reference. If a transaction holds a connection open with an old snapshot, all subsequent checkpoints stall at that frame boundary, causing the WAL file to grow without bound. Documented production cases reach 500MB, 2GB, and 10GB in size; as the WAL swells, every new query suffers degraded performance from searching through the expanded index. You cannot safely deploy WAL without establishing alerting on WAL file size, maximum transaction duration policies, and automatic checkpoint coordination.
